unit_label: Module C unit 3 (courseware unit 19), part 2: discounting of bills, TReDS, non-fund based facilities, commercial paper, factoring and forfaiting

facts.statement: A bank sanctions working capital limits and bills limits only after proper appraisal of credit needs and in accordance with its Board approved policy; the Board approval procedure includes the core operating process from the time bills are tendered until realised, simplified using improved computer and communication networks such as SFMS and the system of value dating of clients' accounts. A bank purchases, discounts or negotiates bills under letters of credit only for genuine commercial and trade transactions of borrower constituents sanctioned regular credit facilities; it does not extend this to non-constituent borrowers or non-constituent members of a consortium or multiple banking arrangement, except that where negotiation of LC bills is restricted to a particular bank and the beneficiary is not its constituent, the bank may negotiate subject to the proceeds being remitted to the beneficiary's regular banker; negotiation of unrestricted LCs of non-constituents is prohibited. A beneficiary may have bills discounted with the LC issuing bank only if that bank has sanctioned regular fund-based credit facilities to the beneficiary. Blank LC forms are kept in safe custody like blank cheques and verified or balanced daily, and are issued under joint signatures of authorised officials.

Bills purchased, discounted or negotiated under an LC where payment to the beneficiary is not made under reserve are treated as an exposure on the LC issuing bank, not on the borrower, and clean negotiations get the risk weight applicable to inter-bank exposures; for negotiations under reserve the exposure is on the borrower and the risk weight follows the borrower; where the negotiating bank and the LC issuing bank are the same bank (for example the LC is issued by its head office or another branch) the exposure is on the third party borrower and not on the LC issuing bank. Banks establish the genuineness of the underlying transactions and documents when purchasing, discounting or negotiating bills.

The practice of drawing bills of exchange claused without recourse, and of issuing LCs bearing the legend without recourse, is discouraged because such notations deprive the negotiating bank of the right of recourse against the drawer under the Negotiable Instruments Act. A bank may negotiate bills drawn under LCs on a with recourse or without recourse basis according to its perception of the credit worthiness of the LC issuing bank, but it does not purchase or discount other bills (not drawn under LC) on a without recourse basis. A bank does not purchase, discount or negotiate accommodation bills; the underlying trade transactions are clearly identified and a proper record is kept at the branches conducting the bills business. A bank is circumspect while discounting bills drawn by front finance companies set up by large industrial groups on other group companies.

Bills rediscount is restricted to usance bills held by other banks; a bank does not rediscount bills earlier discounted by non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), except bills arising from sale of light commercial vehicles and two or three wheelers. A bank exercises commercial judgment in discounting bills of the services sector, ensuring that actual services are rendered and that accommodation bills are not discounted; services sector bills are not eligible for rediscounting, and finance against discounting of services sector bills is treated as unsecured advance and kept within the Board's unsecured exposure norm. To promote payment discipline, all corporates and other constituent borrowers with turnover above a threshold fixed by the bank's Board must disclose an aging schedule of their overdue payables in their periodical returns to the bank. A bank does not enter into repo transactions using bills discounted or rediscounted as collateral.

Under the Non-Fund Based (NFB) Credit Facilities chapter, the bank's credit policy covers the types of NFB facility, limits, credit appraisal, security, fraud prevention, monitoring, delegation, audit and internal controls. A bank issues an NFB facility only on behalf of a customer having a funded credit facility from the bank, except for derivative contracts with a counterparty; partial credit enhancement; facilities issued on the counter guarantee of another regulated entity; facilities for an obligor who has not availed any fund based facility from any regulated entity in India; facilities issued against a No Objection Certificate from the entity providing the fund based facility; and facilities fully secured by eligible financial collateral. A bank does not issue an NFB facility assuring redemption or repayment of funds raised by any entity through deposits, bonds or otherwise unless regulations specifically permit. When an NFB facility devolves and becomes a fund based facility, the prudential norms for fund based facilities apply.

A guarantee (or counter-guarantee) issued by a bank is in general irrevocable (no clause lets the guarantor unilaterally cancel it), unconditional (nothing prevents timely payment if the original counterparty fails), incontrovertible, and contains a clear mechanism for honouring it without demur when invoked. The bank puts in place internal aggregate and individual ceilings for guarantees and especially unsecured guarantees; its policy addresses invocation and settlement, claim period, tenor, fees, release of security, renewal and fraud prevention. The bank honours a guarantee when invoked in accordance with its terms unless a court order restrains it. A bank does not give a guarantee favouring another regulated entity to enable that entity to provide a fund based credit facility to an obligor unless RBI specifically permits (this does not apply to credit facilities against guarantees pertaining to trade related transactions); it may guarantee an NFB facility extended by another entity, which is treated as an exposure on the obligor for all purposes including capital adequacy. Only scheduled commercial banks may issue guarantees on behalf of stock or commodity brokers in favour of exchanges in lieu of security deposit or margin, to the extent acceptable under exchange rules.

For co-acceptance of bills, only genuine trade bills are co-accepted, and the bank ensures that the goods covered are actually received in the borrowers' stock accounts; proper records of bills co-accepted for each customer are kept so that commitments for each customer and total commitments at a branch can be ascertained, and these are part of internal audit; and the bank does not co-accept bills drawn by another lender or where the buyer or seller has received funding for the underlying trade transaction from any lender.

The Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) is a screen-based institutional mechanism for financing trade receivables of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) from corporate and other buyers, including government departments and public sector undertakings, through multiple financiers. It is set up under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (guidelines issued 3 December 2014), facilitates both invoices and bills of exchange and both receivables factoring and reverse factoring, and processes transactions without recourse to the MSME seller. Direct participants are MSME sellers, corporate and other buyers and financiers (banks, NBFC factors and other financial institutions permitted by RBI). By RBI guidelines of 7 June 2023, insurance companies may participate as a fourth participant; premium for insurance is not levied on the MSME seller; collection of premium and related activities can be enabled through NACH; and credit insurance is not treated as a Credit Risk Mitigant (CRM) for prudential benefit.

facts.statement: Commercial paper (CP) is an unsecured money market instrument issued as a promissory note, introduced in 1990 to enable highly rated corporate borrowers to diversify sources of short-term borrowing; primary dealers and all-India financial institutions were later also permitted to issue it. Individuals, banks, other corporate bodies, unincorporated bodies, Non-Resident Indians and Foreign Institutional Investors may invest in CP. The cost of borrowing through CP is normally lower than other sources of short-term finance, so it is a useful working capital management tool.

facts.statement: Factoring is a method of financing the receivables of a business in which the financier, the factor, not only purchases the book debts or receivables of the client but also controls the credit given to the buyers and administers the sales ledger; the purchase may be with recourse or without recourse to the client, and if without recourse the client is not liable to pay the factor if the buyer fails to pay. Banks are permitted to do factoring through subsidiaries or departmentally; factoring services may pay a percentage of the invoice upfront on the basis of an assessment of the creditworthiness of the assignor or buyer. A bank may extend finance to support the factoring business of factoring companies (NBFC-Factors and NBFC-ICCs holding a certificate of registration under the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011) provided the finance is secured by hypothecation or assignment of receivables in their favour and the NBFC-Factor derives at least 50 per cent of its income from factoring and has receivables purchased or financed at least 50 per cent of its assets, excluding any assets and income from bill discounting. Forfaiting is similar to factoring but is used only for exports where the sale is supported by bills of exchange or promissory notes; the financier discounts the bills and collects from the buyer on the due dates, always without recourse to the exporter, so the exporter does not bear the buyer's default risk; EXIM Bank and Authorised Dealer Category-I banks are permitted to undertake forfaiting.

payload.title: Discounting and negotiating bills: who may be financed and where the exposure sits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Policy and process.** Limits for working capital and bills are sanctioned only **after appraisal** and under a **Board approved policy** that covers the bills' journey from tender to realisation. Banks use **SFMS** and **value dating** to cut delay in realisation.

**Bills under LCs**

- Only **genuine trade transactions** of **borrower constituents with regular credit facilities**.
- **Not** for non-constituent borrowers or non-constituent members of a **consortium or multiple banking** arrangement.
- **Exception:** an LC restricted to this bank, beneficiary not a constituent: the bank may negotiate if the **proceeds go to the beneficiary's regular banker**. **Unrestricted LCs** of non-constituents stay **prohibited**.
- A beneficiary discounting with the **LC issuing bank** must have **regular fund-based facilities** with it.

**Where the exposure sits**

| Payment to the beneficiary | Exposure is on | Risk weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Not under reserve** (clean negotiation) | The **LC issuing bank** | **Inter-bank** weight |
| **Under reserve** | The **borrower** | The **borrower's** weight |
| Negotiating bank and LC issuing bank are the **same bank** | The **borrower** | The borrower's weight |

**Controls:** establish the **genuineness** of the underlying transactions and documents; keep **blank LC forms** in safe custody like blank cheques, **balanced daily**, issued under **joint signatures**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This replaces the 2021 master circular reproduced in the courseware; the substance is the same.

self_check.prompt_text: A clean negotiation under an LC: on whom is the exposure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: On the LC issuing bank, with the inter-bank risk weight.

payload.title: Recourse, accommodation bills and rediscounting
payload.core_explanation_md:
**"Without recourse" bills and LCs are discouraged**, because the notation takes away the negotiating bank's **right of recourse against the drawer** under the **Negotiable Instruments Act**.

- **Bills under LCs:** may be negotiated **with or without recourse** depending on the bank's view of the **LC issuing bank's creditworthiness**.
- **Other bills:** **never** on a **without recourse** basis.

**Never:** purchase, discount or negotiate **accommodation bills** (bills with no real trade behind them). Identify the **underlying trade transactions** and keep a **proper record** at branches. Be **circumspect** with bills drawn by **front finance companies** of large groups on **group companies**.

**Rediscounting**

- Only **usance bills held by other banks**.
- Not bills earlier discounted by **NBFCs**, except bills from sale of **light commercial vehicles** and **two or three wheelers**.
- **Services sector bills:** use commercial judgment; ensure **actual services** were rendered; **not eligible for rediscounting**; finance is an **unsecured advance** within the Board's **unsecured exposure** norm.
- **No repo** using bills discounted or rediscounted as collateral.

**Payment discipline:** borrowers above a Board-fixed **turnover threshold** must disclose an **aging schedule** of overdue payables.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Accommodation bills let two parties raise funds without any real sale.

self_check.prompt_text: May a bank discount a non-LC bill on a without-recourse basis?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: only bills drawn under LCs may be negotiated without recourse.

payload.title: The Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**TReDS** is a **screen-based platform** for financing the **trade receivables of MSMEs** from **corporate and government buyers** (including PSUs) through **multiple financiers**.

- Set up under the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007** (guidelines of **3 December 2014**).
- Handles **invoices and bills of exchange**, both **factoring** and **reverse factoring**.
- Transactions are **without recourse to the MSME seller**.
- **Participants:** **MSME sellers**, **buyers**, **financiers** (banks, NBFC factors and other permitted institutions).

**RBI guidelines of 7 June 2023:** **insurance companies** can take part as a **fourth participant**; **no insurance premium on the MSME seller**; premium collection can use **NACH**; **credit insurance is not a Credit Risk Mitigant** for prudential benefit.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The card follows the courseware and is held at needs_review: the guidelines were not checked against RBI texts.

self_check.prompt_text: Does an MSME seller on TReDS carry the buyer's default risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: transactions are without recourse to the MSME seller.

payload.title: Commercial paper, factoring and forfaiting
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Commercial paper (CP):** an **unsecured money market instrument** issued as a **promissory note**, introduced in **1990** so **highly rated corporates** could diversify short-term borrowing. **Primary dealers** and **all-India financial institutions** can also issue. **Investors:** individuals, banks, corporates, unincorporated bodies, **NRIs** and **FIIs**. Its **cost is normally lower** than other short-term finance.

**Factoring:** the **factor** **buys the client's book debts**, **controls credit** to buyers and **runs the sales ledger**.

| | With recourse | Without recourse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If the buyer fails to pay | **Client** must pay the factor | **Factor bears** the loss |

Banks may factor **departmentally or through subsidiaries**.

**Bank finance to factoring companies** (2025 Directions): the finance is **secured by hypothecation or assignment of receivables**, and the **NBFC-Factor** must derive **at least 50 per cent of income from factoring** and have receivables **at least 50 per cent of assets**, **excluding bill discounting**.

**Forfaiting:** like factoring but **only for exports** supported by **bills of exchange or promissory notes**; the financier discounts and collects on due dates, **always without recourse** to the exporter. **EXIM Bank and AD Category-I banks** may undertake it.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware gives 75 per cent for the factoring test (a 2015 circular); the 2025 Directions say 50 per cent.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is always without recourse: factoring or forfaiting?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Forfaiting; factoring may be with or without recourse.

unresolved: Bills discounting, non-fund based facility, guarantee and co-acceptance rules are taught from RBI/DOR/2025-26/154 (paragraphs 144-157, 397-432 read), not from the courseware, which reproduces the 2021 master circular. The copy is the later version (updated October 2026); the pages read carry no amendment after the 30 June 2026 cut-off except the deletion of paragraph 399 from 1 April 2026, which is not used.

Held back, because the 2025 Directions do not carry them in the paragraphs read or they are older circulars not verified: the 10-year maturity guideline for guarantees; the minimum 50 per cent margin and 25 per cent cash margin on guarantees for stock and commodity brokers; the Model Form of Bank Guarantee Bond and DGS&D guarantee details; irrevocable payment commitments for custodian banks; the co-acceptance rule on two officials signing bills of Rs 10,000 and above; the 2016 commercial paper eligibility figures (tangible net worth Rs 4 crore, A3 rating, 7 days to one year); the export factoring on non-recourse basis conditions; rupee denominated trade credit (2019 circular as updated in 2023).

The courseware says a factoring company must derive at least 75 per cent of its income from factoring (RBI circular of 26 November 2015); paragraph 227 of the 2025 Directions says at least 50 per cent of income and at least 50 per cent of assets, so the 2025 figures are taught.

The Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) account (2014 guidelines and the 7 June 2023 insurance changes) is the courseware's; TReDS is not mentioned in the 2025 Credit Facilities Directions and no primary source was retrieved (facts marked needs_review).
